utterances.text: How would you characterise the relations that you had with Vlatko Kupreskic and his family?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: Yes. They were good, good relations. But Vlatko likes to work a lot, he likes business, so he had less time for us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Today, the relations with the family of Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic, have they continued?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Today or recently, have you been in contact with Zoran and Mirjan, either by letter or by telephone?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: No, unfortunately not. I'm very sorry that I hadn't even sent a Christmas card. I had a lot of work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, I would like to now turn to the climate that was in Ahmici, Santici, and Pirici before the month of April 1993. It seems to me that you stated that, on several occasions before the month of April 1993 and even before October 1992, you saw groups of armed Muslims, in particular, around the mosque. Did I understand your statement correctly?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: Well, I didn't specify what time that was and how many times because I don't remember exactly, but I saw them often, generally near the mosque, because that was a direction that was necessary for me every day. I would pass that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Therefore, to the best of your knowledge, there was a frequent presence of armed Muslims around the mosque?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, you did not see and you could not see armed Croats in the village of Ahmici or Santici and, even less so, groups of armed Croats?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I think that I was clear enough. The section of the road that I was taking is -- my mother's house is the first house, so I didn't have the opportunity. Even if there had been any, I didn't have the opportunity to see any.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your mind, given the results of that situation, the presence of armed Muslims and the absence of armed Croats, did this create an imbalance which perhaps was a provocation and a threat to your own security?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: Yes. It was terrible. In the last few months, the number of the citizens in Ahmici grew; it almost doubled. Of course, this frightened me, in view of the fact that I lived alone with my mother.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Therefore, within the last months that preceded April 1993, you felt terrorised and extremely threatened by the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I didn't say that. I was just afraid. But direct threats with regard to me and my mother, there had been no direct threats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What exactly were you afraid of, Madam?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: I was afraid -- well, I'll give you an example. When they would come back from the front, they would shoot, and also the group itself. In view of the fact that I'm a woman and I would pass by five or six of them and they had arms, of course, I would be afraid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, I'm trying to understand. The men who you would see, the armed men, you said that they were coming from the front.

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The front against the Serbs, they were fighting against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Serbs were a common enemy. The Muslims were fighting against your common enemy. How would such a situation threaten your security or cause you to be afraid when they returned from the front?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: Well, look, I don't know what their reason was for shooting, but when a rifle fires, I get afraid, regardless of the reason why it was fired. So, of course, I can't define that, what you're asking me. I don't know why and against who they fought. I only heard that from talk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you never see Croatians or Croats, rather, returning from the front?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: No, I didn't see that because we did not have a man in the house. So it wasn't something that was of particular interest to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But there were Croats living in the houses around your own. Did you never see any Croats or did you not know of any Croats coming from the front?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: The Croats who lived close to my house, as far as I know, did not go to any front. Well, I say that, as much as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's now turn to the events in October of 1992. You stated a moment ago that you do not remember that the Muslims had left Ahmici and only returned a few days later. Do you remember at least the discussions which took place at that time between the representatives of the Croatian community and representatives from the Muslim community concerning the conditions for their return and the conditions for the establishment of peace and trust between those two communities; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: Well, I've already said that the part that I would pass through, I didn't notice that the Muslims had moved away. All those agreements I was not aware of. I didn't know that and I was not familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your friend, Zoran Kupreskic, never talk to you about these discussions, about these agreements, and the return of Muslims?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: No. No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you never heard it said that the Muslims living in Ahmici were asked to give their weapons, to surrender their weapons to the Croats?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that. I can't remember that anybody ever in my presence talked about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your own mind, at the end of the conflict on the 20th of October, 1992, was there a victor in that conflict?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: I don't know. Believe me, I don't even know who started it, who was firing, and who ended it. I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A moment ago, you mentioned a group of soldiers, some wearing uniforms and others in civilian clothing, that you saw on the road near your house, and this group was led by Fuad Berbic.

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It seems that you had a very exact memory of this because you named nine other persons, Muslims, who were in this group. Since your memory of this is very sharp and you remember the names of persons in this group, can you please tell me what that group was doing on that road at the time in which you saw them?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: I only met them, and, of course, I stopped so that all of them could pass. Where they went after that and what they did, as far as I remember, I didn't say that the first time either; I didn't know what their objective was, and, of course, I didn't ask them. I only greeted them. I've already said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Perhaps this might be a good time to adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Terrier?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, I would like to return for a few moments to the group led by Mr. Fuad Berbic that you saw on the road. You don't remember at all what they were doing on the road?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: I met them. They were just walking along. I didn't see any more than that. I didn't see what they were doing, their objective, or where they were going. I stopped so that they could pass by, and I have already said that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they weren't doing anything in particular. They weren't firing. You could not guess what their intentions might be. Nonetheless, you said that their simple presence frightened you a great deal.

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: They weren't firing, but there were a lot of them, yes. I stopped. They frightened me because they were all carrying weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, how can you be sure that this took place in mid November 1992, as you stated?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: Well, I didn't specify the time or the day, but I think that I said that this was in mid November. I don't know exactly what date, what day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, I'm not going to ask you for the exact day, but I would like to know the period. How can you be certain that it was in mid November 1992 when this took place and not in October or perhaps in September 1992?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: I remembered it because the first conflict occurred before that, yes, on the 20th of October.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Therefore, you are absolutely certain that the scene that you described took place after the 20th of October, 1992?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, I'm asking you this question because the Tribunal received several statements from Croat and Muslim witnesses who stated that, after the Muslims returned to Ahmici, that no activities of this type were noted by them.

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: Well, I saw that group, and after that and before, I didn't happen to see them. Whether they gathered in those groups before or after, I don't know that. I'm only talking about what I saw in that period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But is it impossible that you saw this group before October 1992?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: Well, it's possible that they grouped, but I didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, let's return to the day of the 20th of October, 1992. If I correctly understood your testimony, you left your house with your mother to seek shelter at your house, Vidovic, and that in this shelter, you encountered five armed Muslims who were dressed in uniforms; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I said that of the five of them, two of them had uniforms and the other three were wearing civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, you're correct. I'm sorry. I apologise. Nonetheless, there were five Muslims, all armed?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you specify at what time these five Muslims entered the shelter?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: I can't say that more specifically because I didn't have a watch, and I didn't see them when they arrived to the shelter. I only already met them in the shelter. I found them in the shelter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived in this shelter, what was the general situation? Was there firing? Could you hear any exchange of canon fire or rifle fire around the road or in the area of Vitez, the road leading to Vitez? What was the situation at the time?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: Yes, there was firing, and that's why we went to the shelter. I don't know. I couldn't determine now from which direction the shooting came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If there was shooting, could you draw the conclusion then that there was fighting?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know whether there was fighting. I know that there was shooting. I couldn't see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If there is shooting, perhaps you wouldn't be too far off to conclude that there was fighting; do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: Yes, probably, but I don't know what the reasons would be for the shooting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The five Muslims in the shelter, were they taking shelter in order to escape the fighting, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I think I said that, what their intention was, their reason for being there, but they weren't provoking my mother or myself. They were even kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You weren't frightened by their presence then?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: I was frightened when I was going in, but later, I wasn't because we had no choice. What was there was there. If they had wanted to, they could have done anything to us, but they were very correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you thought that these five Muslim soldiers were hiding at the moment of this fighting and what might have been fighting were harmless?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: At that time, I wasn't thinking at all. We had taken refuge there, and I didn't feel that I was in danger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time in October or November 1992 or in the ensuing months until 1993, did you see or hear the village guard made up of empowered Croats and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: In view of the fact that the time period was the autumn, going onto winter, yes. In the evening, when I would come home from work at 6.00 p.m., I had the opportunity to see them in groups, most frequently near the mosque, but I didn't go further into the village because there was no need for me to go further.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The persons you just mentioned, were they Muslims or Croats or a mixture of Croats and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: I think that they were Muslims because they were on the side where the Muslim inhabitants were. That road, in fact, divides Ahmici and Pirici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So at that time then, you had no knowledge of any guard made up of Croats?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You never saw them and no one ever talked to you about them?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: No. I didn't pay much attention to that because, as I have already mentioned, I lived alone with my mother, and I didn't know anything about it. I couldn't say anything about it specifically.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You just stated and you stated earlier that you were living alone with your mother, that in this village, you saw a number of events which frightened you and which frightened you given your situation. You had no knowledge of any reassuring presence of Croats, and you did not seek any information, for example, from your friend Zoran Kupreskic, to find out what was happening, to find out whether the Croats who were guaranteeing the security of the Croats in the village, you did not look for any information of this type at all?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: Well, you see all the insecurity that I felt at that time I regularly communicated to my brother, Rudo Vidovic, and if anything happened anywhere in the surrounding area, for example, in Bugojno, he would always come and tell us to go to the houses of the Kupreskics. So I did not feel any need to talk to Zoran about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A moment ago, I believe we referred to November 1992, when you mentioned a false alert, false alarm. You said that it was stated that the Mujahedeen were located in Barin Gaj and that, therefore, you had to seek shelter. Do you remember that episode?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: Yes, I remember it very well. It was after 11.00 p.m. when my relative, Miro Vidovic, rang us up on the telephone and told us that 50 Mujahedeen had arrived in Barin Gaj. Of course, in few of the circumstances, I took my mother and the cow, and we set off toward the shelter. We arrived at the house of Niko Sakic, and my mother said, "Let's go home. Who could have counted them at this time of night?" Of course, my mother was right because on that evening, nothing happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words, that was incorrect information?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, your relative that alerted you by telephone, what happened in that episode?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: No, I don't -- we weren't given any detailed explanations. He only said what I told you, that the Mujahedeen had arrived and that we had to flee.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, at that time, discuss with other persons, Zoran or Mirjan Kupreskic, this feeling of insecurity that you had, this feeling that there was mounting tension in the village between the two communities?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: Well, there was talk about this because all the villagers living in this area noticed that, from day to day, the population was growing, but the explanation was that these were all refugees coming in because, as far as I can remember, sometime around October, Jajce fell, and a lot of these people were allegedly from there. But we did not discuss any specific details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your mother, for example, have the feeling that, due to the situation and due to the presence of Mujahedeen in the area and due to the influx of Muslim refugees who were settling in Ahmici, that her situation, her own personal safety was threatened? Did your mother have the same feelings that you did?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: No. My mother is very old, and she's a very placid woman. She was not frightened by any of this information. For example, when I told you about the Mujahedeen, my mother would always go to the shelter for my sake.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of any explicit threats that were made against the Croat numbers of Ahmici or Croats in the area at that time, threats that might explain the feeling that you had that your safety was threatened?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: I personally, personally, did not have any threats made against me. So that I didn't feel so imperilled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the persons who you may have met during the course of your work in Ahmici, your friends, or the information that you may have learned by watching television, if you had a television, or perhaps a radio, if you had a radio, or perhaps by reading the newspapers, did all of this give you the feeling that your security was threatened by the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: Well, for example, in Dusina, something happened. I don't know exactly when or where, but whenever I heard something of that kind, I felt afraid, but I was convinced, since I was a local villager and I lived there -- in general, to put it briefly, I was in two minds. There were times when I would get frightened by all these events, and then I would feel I had to come back again because I had no other home then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, let us now move on to the evening of the 15th of April, 1993. You told us that you returned to your home after work at 6.00 p.m. and that you went to the house of your friend Zoran Kupreskic. Did your mother come with you?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the testimony during examination in chief by Mr. Radovic, you stated that during that visit on the 15th, on the evening of the 15th, that the village of Kovacevac, that there we can see houses burning, and that you had seen this from the house of Zoran. Can you please explain your memory of this event?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: Well, just as Mr. Radovic wrote down, all I could do was to see. I don't know any other details about it because --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please confirm that when you went to visit Zoran Kupreskic on the 15th of April, in the evening, around 7.00 p.m., I believe, that the village of Kovacevac was burning?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: I think, as far as I remember, that it was, but that village is quite far from the spot where I was standing and from which I could see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where is this village, Kovacevac, located, exactly?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: It's parallel -- from the house of Zoran Kupreskic you can see it, but it belongs to the municipality of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far is it from Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to estimate this, because the terrain is hilly, so I couldn't say precisely what the distance is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why, in your opinion, what was your opinion as to why this village was burning on the 15th in the evening?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly what I thought then. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this something habitual, normal, to see a village burning?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: No. No. It wasn't something usual. When there is a big fire -- but whether it was the village that was burning or the woods around the village, I don't know. Something was burning, but I wasn't able to see exactly what it was because it's quite far. I couldn't see precisely what was burning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you speak with Zoran Kupreskic about this?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: No. I didn't attach any special importance to it because they had probably seen it too. I don't know how much importance they attached to it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who lived in the village of Kovacevac? Was it a Muslim or a Croat village?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I don't know who lived there, what kind of people. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in summary, madam, when you arrived at the home of Zoran Kupreskic, you saw the village of Kovacevac on fire, but you attached no great importance to that, and therefore you said nothing to Zoran Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: No, I don't remember saying anything about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that during the course of that evening you, together with Zoran Kupreskic, visited Ivica -- rather together with Ivica Kupresic, and that you remained there for a very short time period. Can you please tell us what that means, when you say you were there for a very short time period. Does that mean 5 minutes, 15 minutes, perhaps half an hour, or an hour and a half? When you say "a short time," what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: So short that we only said hello to her, because she hadn't been here for a long time, and then we went back to Zoran's house immediately. I can't say whether it was two minutes or five minutes or ten minutes; I don't know exactly. But it was very, very brief.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, if you only came to say hello and to leave, that would be a very short visit. But how can you be certain and so specific about what persons were there?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: Well, since the living room was rather small, there was not enough room for us to sit down. We might have stayed longer otherwise. So I saw who was inside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But is it possible that other persons were in other rooms? For example, in the kitchen?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: I don't believe so. I didn't see them, because it's all interconnected, but I didn't see any other people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you cannot exclude the fact that some persons may have come and gone before your visit, or perhaps after that, of course?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't pay attention to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the house of Zoran Kupreskic on that evening, your mother and yourself were invited, but were there also other persons?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: There were Zoran's parents, and my mother, and briefly Mirjan with his wife, but they had to leave because his child was ill, so they had to go home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mirjan come with you to visit Ivica Kupreskic and his wife?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: I have already said, I think I remember well, I said it was only with Zoran that I went to see Ankica, and Mirjan was already there. In the meantime, he went back again, but not with us, together with us, as far as I can remember, to Zoran's house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that evening, do you remember that the telephone rang at Zoran's house and that there was a telephone conversation?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: No, I don't remember. Because that evening we were watching a very interesting tape, and I was concentrating on that. So there might have been a telephone call, but I didn't notice one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was on this videotape that you looked at?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: Mostly music. It was mostly music.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You stated a moment ago that on the 16th of April, in the morning, that you were awakened by Dragan Vidovic. You aren't able to specify the time at which you were awakened by Mr. Vidovic, but you were quite certain, as you stated, that it was after 4.00 in the morning. How can you be so clear on this point, since you did not know what time it was at that time?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: I know because we arrived at the shelter -- my mother is old, so she needed more time than I did. Then I asked the people who were already at the shelter what time it was, and it was about 5.00 a.m., as far as I remember. Whether it was quarter past 5.00 or exactly 5.00, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's because, therefore, that you knew that you arrived at the shelter at 5.00 or 5.15 that you knew how much time you took to arrive at that shelter, and based on that, you knew you were awakened around 4.00 in the morning, or around that time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: Yes, it would be logical to think that. 4.00, sometime after 4.00. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any family relations with Dragan Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is that relationship?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: He's the son of my half-uncle, step-uncle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where does he live in Ahmici? Where was he living at that time? Where?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: Near my house. Quite close. Quite close.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You saw him on that morning, you spoke with him, did you not?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: No. He woke us up and said, without any explanation, for me to take my mother and to go to the shelter. And he left. I don't know where.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you saw him, did you not?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I opened the door. Of course, I asked who was it, and then I opened the door, and I saw him. Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was he dressed, to the best of your recollection? Was he wearing a uniform, or was he wearing civilian clothing?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly what he was wearing, because I had just gotten up. I was afraid. I didn't know who would be ringing at the doorbell at that time, so I don't remember what he was wearing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember whether or not he had a weapon?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: No, I don't remember. I had just woken up, so I don't know what he had. It was just him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is he the one who told you to go to the shelter in the house of Vrebac, or were you the one that took that decision?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: I made that decision. He didn't say anything. He didn't give any explanations, like I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why, then, did you decide to go to the shelter in Jozo Vrebac's house and not something closer to your own home: For example, the house where you took shelter in October 1992, at the house of Mr. Sakic, or where you intended to go when there was that false alarm about the presence of the Mujahedeen? Why, then, off to the shelter in Jozo Vrebac's house?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: There's a larger settlement there, around Jozo Vrebac's house. Since it was morning and I had just woken up and I wanted to go as far as possible, and then I stopped at the shelter of Jozo Vrebac. I didn't think which was closer, in order to go to Rudo's house, my brother's house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please clarify something for me. I'm trying to understand. You said you decided to go to the Vrebac shelter because you thought that would be safer than others. However, at the same time, that shelter was located in an area in Santici and Ahmici which is almost exclusively inhabited by Croats. But, madam, if you felt that the Muslims were going to attack, do you think it is reasonable to believe that they were going to attack the areas inhabited by the Muslims, or the Croats?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: At that time, I didn't think about anything. I just went to the shelter. And I can't remember what I was thinking about at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, isn't it reasonable to think -- rather, you decided not to go to the Vidovic shelter and not to go to any other shelter, but rather to go as far as possible to the Vrebac shelter, which is as far as possible from your own home? And you did this because you were told or because you learned that a fight would be taking place in the Muslim area of Ahmici, is that what you are telling me, and not to the Croat area?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: I've already said that at that time, I wasn't thinking anything specific.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please specify which path you used in order to go to the Vrebac shelter from your house? And if you like, would you please show us the path on this photograph.

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: This is my house (indicating). Just below my house there is a depression, it's a field. Then there's a shortcut, and it comes out exactly at Niko Sakic's house. Then I go further, I carry on, and then here (indicating) -- I can't indicate precisely here, I've already said around Pudza houses, I caught up with Zoran and his family, Mirjan and his family, and the grandmother that they were pushing in a wheelbarrow. So we passed them and went to the house of Jozo Vrebac. That's --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, did you encounter any soldiers?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: (No audible response)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, madam, be seated. You may be seated. Madam, on this path that you just pointed out which you took from the house of Niko Sakic to the shelter of Jozo Vrebac, you encountered and passed the family of Zoran Kupreskic. Now, were there soldiers in that location, on that path?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: No, I didn't encounter anybody.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will now ask for the usher to show the witness Defence Exhibit D14/1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, does this photograph indeed show the house of Jozo Vrebac in which you took shelter on the 16th of April, in the morning?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And looking at this photograph, with numbers 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, and 7, can you show us the path that you took, you and your mother, to arrive at this house?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: As far as I can see, you can only see the house and the rooms where we were during the time that there was gunfire. And there is no road here that I could show you. I've already done that on the map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, perhaps I did not express myself clearly. I would like for you to show us, if possible, on these photographs, the place at which you took shelter, you arrived at this house with your mother, and I believe that you entered that house, and then you went somewhere in that house. Can we see on this photograph where, exactly, you went?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: Yes. You can see -- if I can see my way around here -- well, there's the front hall (indicating). Then there's a smaller room and a larger room. I put my mother in the larger room, and from time to time I was in one and in the other, and in the third room, in order to give room to the children and the elderly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, it was indicated to me that there was no response on the transcript when I asked whether or not the witness had seen soldiers on the path leading to Jozo Vrebac's home. Perhaps all we need is to specify that she stated that she did not see the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, you are now showing us a very large room in which -- or do you see a large room on these photographs where you and your mother were located? And if so, can you please tell us what number corresponds with that.

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: Yes, I think, as far as I remember, that this is the large room (indicating). And it's under number 5. But I'm not sure. I can only see a part of it here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But in the basement of this house, were there several rooms, as we see them here?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: Yes, I told you there were several rooms. There was the front hall, a smaller room, and a larger room. But I can't tell exactly, with these photographs here, which of these rooms is the largest, so I came to the conclusion that it must be under number 5.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived in that room, were there already people there?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: Yes. There were a lot of people. A lot of children. And adults, men and women. And I don't remember exactly who was there, but I could mention a few of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you simply tell us which people were there? Of those you remember, that is.

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: Ivo Vidovic, Alojz Vidovic, Marko Livancic, the Marjanovic family -- when I say "family," I mean everybody was there. Ljuba Vidovic, Lucija Papic, the Omazics -- just their surname, and so on. I can't remember exactly who was there, but there were a lot of people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall seeing on that morning, when you arrived or later, Ankica Kupreskic, the wife of Ivica?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: I saw them, but whether they were already there when I arrived, whether they were there after or before I came, I don't remember, but they were there when I was there. I don't remember if they came before I did or after me, but I remember they were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any light in the shelter?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: At the time that I arrived there was, but later there wasn't, no. So after that, there wasn't. I can't tell after how much time the light was cut, after half an hour or 15 minutes, but within a short period of time, the electricity was cut.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when the electricity was cut, could you see then what was going on in this basement?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: Some of those present had something, they had candles, I don't remember what it was. But it had already started to get light, and there were small windows where the light came, but not to an extent that you could read by it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these lanterns that we see in the photograph on number 7 -- rather these windows, weren't they blocked by boards? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: Well, I didn't pay any particular attention to the window. I don't remember. I didn't really pay any special attention to the windows.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In these rooms, were there mattresses, so that children or elderly persons could lie down?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: There was something, I don't know exactly what, but mainly the elderly were sitting on something, but I don't know exactly what that was, because I wasn't sitting, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Given the way this room was arranged, did you have the impression that this room had been prepared to receive you?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: I don't know what I was thinking at that time. It was important for me to find a place for my mother to sit down. Whether it was prepared or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You stated a moment ago that you left the shelter at 10.00. From the time of your arrival and the time of your departure at 10.00, did you remain in that one room the entire time?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: No. No, from time to time, I would go because all the people who were there were known to me. From time to time, I would go out and in from one room to another.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During that entire period, did you remain in the basement or did you leave the house?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: From the basement, I didn't go up the stairs, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We see on picture number 3 a photograph of a stairwell. You state that from the time you arrived, which was at 5.00 or 5.15 in the morning, until the moment you left at 10.00, you stayed in the basement and did not climb the stairs.

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: No, I didn't climb the stairs or go outside to the terrace that is shown on this photograph until about 10.00 or sometime after when I went to my house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, you stated a moment ago that you saw Vlatko Kupreskic and his family arrive last, I add, in the shelter shortly after the shooting had begun, and you exchanged a few words with Vlatko Kupreskic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Vlatko Kupreskic explain why his father was not there?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: Yes. I asked him, and he said that he was sick and that, allegedly, if something happens, the Muslims would not harm him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Vlatko Kupreskic had no concerns about the safety of his father? His father was not at risk where he was?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: I wouldn't know. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Until the time at which you left the shelter at 10.00, would you see Vlatko Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: Yes. During the time I was there, he was in the shelter all the time. In which room he was exactly, I don't know. I don't know which one I was in exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're telling us then that, between the arrival of Vlatko Kupreskic and his family at the shelter and the time at which you left at 10.00, he remained, like you, in the basement of the house?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he was still there when you left?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: I don't know. I came back. I don't know how long I stayed away. I was frightened when I saw them carrying Mirjan Santic along, and by the time I recovered from this shock -- I came back, I don't know what time it was -- but Vlatko wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. He was still there when you left at 10.00, and when you returned, he was no longer there?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the apparent situation in Ahmici when you left from the shelter, that is, around 10.00, according to your estimations? Could one hear firing or what could one see?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, there was gunfire, but the houses are close to one another in the part I was going through. Then I ran across to Niko's house, and I didn't go further.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What would you see that was happening around you at that time?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: I couldn't see anything, except that I heard the gunfire. I just heard it. I didn't see anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll clarify my question. Did you not see in Ahmici houses burning at that time?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: When I was passing through at about 10.00, I didn't look. I was running because there was gunfire, and I don't remember noticing that at that moment. But on the 17th, when I came home again, then I saw that the houses had been burnt, that they were charred, and I was able to see this from my mother's house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But at that time, at 10.00 on the 16th of April, while you were on the road leading to the house of Niko Santic -- was it Mirko Santic or Niko Santic?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: -- Niko Santic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did not see any houses burning, either around you or further afield in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: No, I couldn't see because I was moving through an area from which I couldn't see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe you stated this a moment ago, but could you please remind us of why you decided to turn around on that road at 10.00.

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: I became frightened when I saw them carrying a corpse because I'm terrified of corpses. I couldn't bear to look at my dead father's body either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's because you saw the dead body of Mirjan Santic that you returned to the shelter?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: Yes. I returned, but Mirko Sakic was nearby, and he told me that there was gunfire and that I couldn't go further in that direction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned a moment ago that the body of Mirjan Santic had a blue scarf. What exactly was that?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: You see, I saw the corpse on a ladder, and I only noticed that, around his neck, there was a pale blue scarf, and I saw nothing else at that moment. I don't remember anything else. I asked Mirko, "Who is this?" And he told me it was Mirjan Santic. I didn't see the scarf on his body but around his neck.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. You recall seeing Nikola Omazic; you mentioned his name a moment ago. Do you remember how he was dressed?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: In civilian clothes, civilian clothes, as far as I can remember, but I think I remember well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember whether he had a weapon?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't know. I don't know about weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you turned around at that time and returned to the shelter in Vrebac's house. Do you remember exactly what path you took?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you stay on the same path that you showed to us a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that path, on your way back to the Vrebac shelter, did you encounter Vlatko Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I didn't meet him, but there are several directions where he and I might have passed one another, and I don't know when he left the shelter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nonetheless, from the moment you left the shelter, let's say it was around 10.00, and the time in which you returned to the shelter, how much time may have elapsed? I'm asking you for an approximation. I'm not asking you for the exact time. How much time do you believe it took for you to go from the Vrebac shelter to the house of Nikola Omazic and to return? Would it take 5 minutes, 20 minutes? I'm asking for just an approximation.

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: Maybe my estimate is 40 to 50 minutes, but I don't know. I don't know. I can't specify the exact amount of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us a moment ago that, during the day that you spent in the Vrebac shelter, food was brought to you, that Zoran brought food. Where did this food come from?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: At the house of Ivica Kupreskic, there were two grandmothers, Ivica's aunt and a refugee who was in the house of Branko Kupreskic and Josip Kupreskic. They were elderly women, and, at that time, they were not in the shelter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you know that these two people had stayed in the house to do the cooking?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: When they brought in the food, I asked one of them -- I don't remember exactly whether I asked Ivica or Mirjan -- who prepared the food, and then they told me that these two women had stayed there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From what you learned at that time, from the discussions that you had with Zoran and Ivica Kupreskic, it seemed to you that these two women had remained in order to prepare food for all the refugees?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: I don't know that, but that's all they told me. What their purpose was in remaining behind, I don't know, but if it hadn't been for me, my mother would not have left her house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When, during that day, did you go to the house of Milutin Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: Early in the morning, when I had only just arrived in the shelter, I left my mother there and I went back to Milutin Vidovic's house because it's very nearby.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Therefore, that was before 10.00 in the morning?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: It was early in the morning. I had only just arrived. Whether it was 6.00 or 5.00 or half past five, I don't know, but it was immediately. I left my mother, as I said, and I went back to see where Mirjan's wife was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You stated a moment ago that you stated that, from the time you arrived in the shelter to the time you left the shelter, you remained in the basement.

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I've forgotten that. I forgot to say that, I mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you see in the house of Milutin Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: There was Zoran Kupreskic's wife and her children. There were refugees. There was Manda Didak, Marica Didak with her children. There was Milutin's wife, Jasna, she was there, and I think that Jasna Safradin was there too, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, please don't say if you don't know, but do you know what time you arrived at the house of Milutin Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know exactly what time it was, but it was early, as soon as I left my mother. I don't know exactly when it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, you stated a moment ago that when you returned to your house the following day, on the 17th of April, 1993, with the intention of milking the cow, you stated that at that time you noted that all the houses had been burned, but had all the houses truly been burned?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: You see, I didn't say they were in flames. What I saw was that they had already been burnt, that they were charred. Whether they had burnt during the night or that evening, I don't know. But Smajl Pezer's house, of which I have a very good view and which is nearby, had been burnt down and so had the house of Sulejman Pezer. I can see that from my mother's house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see a house belonging to a Croat which was burned or damaged?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: No, I didn't along the route I passed along, and I didn't go any further at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam. Mr. President, I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I will put only a few brief questions to the witness. Re-examined by Mr. Radovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please sit down. In the area of Vitez, was it usual for women to be involved in political and military issues or was this exceptional?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: In the circle in which I moved, the women were not interested in politics, and I don't know about other people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you a member of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At any moment?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to the Prosecutor's question, you will have to explain further because it's remained unclear. You were asked how you knew that the Muslims were preparing to attack the Croats or the Croatian houses, and you sought refuge in a Croatian house, even though you knew that Croatian houses would be attacked. According to the Prosecutor, you should have gone to a Muslim house to seek refuge. Why didn't you do that?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me repeat it. According to the Prosecutor's question, you had information that Croatian houses were to be attacked by Muslims. The information was that the Muslims would attack Croats. Wait. Wait. Now, the Prosecutor is asking you, if you knew that the Croats were to be attacked, why did you seek refuge in Croatian houses rather than in Muslim houses?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: Well, it's logical that I should go to the Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: Well, I'm not -- for God's sake, I'm not going to take refuge in Muslim houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. That's clear. We needn't go into that further.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I must object to the formation of the question he put to the witness. I understand, of course, that he would ask such a question, but I would like to remind this Court that that was not the sense of my question. I was not asking why she took refuge in a Croat and not a Muslim house, but rather I was referring to the area in which there were Croat and Muslim houses. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: If I misunderstood the Prosecutor's question, I apologise, but I put the question in the way I understood it. So we can proceed further now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you saw flames and you thought that they were in the village of Kovacevac; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the spot from which you could see the flames, could you see what was on fire?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: No. As I said, I couldn't see what was on fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it the season of the year when weeds are cleaned?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How is that done in that region?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: Well, all the weeds are burnt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any cases when a wood would catch fire?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: Yes, very often.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what the flames were?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the end, I would like to ask something about the shelter because we talked about whether the shelter was prepared or not. The Prosecutor mentioned mattresses, and you said that there had been some things which were not mattresses, but there was something there.

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: Yes, there was something there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, can you explain anything that was there?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what there was. There was something you could sit on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you sit in the Bosnian way on the floor or did you sit on chairs or benches?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: There was something there. I think they were chairs. We didn't sit on the floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's talk about a prepared shelter. Were there any food supplies in the shelter?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any water supplies there?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any blankets?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any beds, bunk-beds, where you could sleep?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there anything there that would indicate that this was a prepared shelter?

utterances.speaker: GORDANA CUIC.
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mrs. Cuic, thank you for coming to The Hague to testify in court. You may now be released. Thank you. I suggest that we take a break now, a 15-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Sakic? Mr. Sakic. Good morning. Could you please make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. Counsel Slokovic-Glumac?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I just wanted to say before I start questioning that the attorneys for Vlatko Kupreskic would like to examine this witness because he is also a witness from their defence. He is on their list.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Examined by Ms. Slokovic-Glumac:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sakic, good day.

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please introduce yourself to the Court?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: My name is Niko Sakic. I was born on the 25th of September, 1939, in the village of Pirici, where I am living today, municipality of Vitez, Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that you live in Pirici?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please indicate that on the aerial map? Could you please point your house out?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: My house is at the moment here (indicating). Here it is. This is my house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Who lived with you in that house in '91, '92, and '93?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: I lived on the first floor, on the ground floor, on the first floor, with an entrance on the other side lived my son and his family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the name of your son?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: His name is Mirko Sakic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the house of your other son close by?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: Yes, this is where the house of my other son is, on the other side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the name of your other son?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: That son is called Slavko Sakic, who lived with his family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Why did you say that it's currently your house? Was it somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: Yes, I had a house a little lower down, but in 1985 I moved 200 metres further, I made a house in a nicer place, and that's the house where I'm living now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sakic, would you please show us where your first Muslim neighbours were in relation to your house.

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: In relation to my house, my first Muslim neighbours -- well, here it's Refik Ahmic and Sulejman Ahmic. My late father took some land from them and an old house which we later then knocked down when we were making this one. Then further down I had neighbours, Ramo and Zijad, and a brother of theirs who is working in Austria. These are my closest Muslim neighbours, that are closest to my house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the other houses are Croatian; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: Yes, along this road, they're all Croatian houses, and then here there are two Muslim homes. But in this direction, there are no more close to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What part of those villages, Pirici, Ahmici, and Santici, was exclusively Muslim? Could you please point that out?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: This part was exclusively Muslim. This is the main road, Travnik, Vitez, Sarajevo, and then here (indicating), on the left side, is the school here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's the road that goes to Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: Yes, the road that goes to Ahmici. On the right side, going towards Ahmici, there was exclusively Muslim population, up until the warehouse of Vlatko Kupreskic. Then up here (indicating) you have two Kupreskic houses and then this road here (indicating) and this settlement is 100 per cent Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So when you go in the direction from Vitez towards Busovaca, on the left side, you would turn to Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: Then the Muslim homes are here, and then up until the school here, there are three, four houses on the left side, and then the rest are all Muslim houses on the right side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Would you please sit down. You said that you were born in Pirici?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were your relations with Muslims since you were born and since your parents were there and they lived with them? What were the relations, the generational relations?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: Well, I personally never had a quarrel with a single Muslim. Regarding relations, they were the same as the ones with the Croats, but you knew who was a Muslim by religion and who was a Croat by religion. We had a tradition which -- well, a neighbour of mine, who was a good friend with my father, they would bring us gifts for Bajram, and we would take them gifts for Easter. Then they died, but we continued, Esad Ahmic and myself exchanged gifts right up until the conflict, and we exchanged visits. The conflict occurred on the 16th, and then on the 11th it was our Easter, and I went to Esad Ahmic and I took him some painted eggs or something, and I had some coffee at his house, I had some cakes, and then I went home. They would come for coffee. We were friends. Pjanic Hajrudin, Sulejman Ahmic, Refik Ahmic, Hazim Ahmic. These were family friends. Of course not all the Muslims were our family friends, just like not all Croats are my family friends.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you bring your sons up, Slavko and Mirko? Did you bring them up to respect another religion, their customs, in the same way that you did?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: Well, of course. They never had any conflicts with Muslims, and further along in my story I will tell you where my son and the son of Ljubo Vidovic and Mr. Bruno Buzuk where they took Ramo Ramic, his wife -- Mejra, I think her name was -- and their family, they took them to Zenica. What I want to say is that my children never thought of doing any harm to Muslims, of making any trouble for them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Did you know about the roadblock on the 15th of 1992, that there was a roadblock set up on the Vitez-Busovaca road?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: I didn't know about it, but I had heard that there had been a roadblock. I didn't see it, but I heard that there was one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you hear?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: I heard that same day, maybe at about 9.00 or 10.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who told you about it?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: I don't remember now who told me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did you have any information that because of that roadblock there would be some problems, some conflicts, on the 19th of October?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: Well, when I heard that, there was talk that there was a Muslim army which had set up the roadblock and that some danger would come from there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what happened in the morning of the 20th of October?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: On the 20th of October, at 4.00 a.m., I was woken up by Jozo Tomic Dobac. That family has two last names; I don't know which is their official one. And he told me like this: He had seen or heard that there was a lot of armed soldiers on the roads and that it would be a good thing to go to the shelter. Of course I woke up my family. I woke up my son Mirko, his family, my son Slavko and his family, and my closest neighbours, Nikola Samija and his family, Nikola Omazic and his family, Drago Grgic and his family, Miro Samija and his family, Milan Samija, also his family, Anto Pudza and Slavko Pudza with their families, who came to my basement to seek refuge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the persons that you mentioned now, the Samijas, the Grbics, the Pudzas, and I don't know who else, the Omazics?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: Yes, the Omazics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were the homes of those people?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: Well, Milan Samija's house is maybe 120 or 150 metres away from my house, and the others have homes which are even closer to mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So these are your immediate neighbours?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: Yes. And they still live there today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you go to inform those people about what you had heard, that there was some army on the road? Why did you do that?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: Well, when the bombardment started in Busovaca and Vitez, we organised ourselves in such a way so that there is somebody who can inform the people, to alert them, so that not everybody would go. I was a member of the civilian defence, so everybody was assigned about 10 or 15 houses that they could inform easily for people to take shelter in case of need.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this was a kind of civil defence duty?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: Yes, I was a kind of civil defence member, and this is what we did, because we decided it was easy for everybody to inform 10 or 15 homes, depending on how densely their area was populated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were in charge of that area immediately around your house?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So how many houses is that, the ones that you mentioned? About ten?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: Yes, about ten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you informed those people, then what happened?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: Well, when they all came -- I don't know whether they all came, but most of the women and the children and the elderly, when they came, then I came out in front of my house with my son Mirko, because I had heard from the direction of the school or the cemetery -- should I indicate that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. No, we know where the cemetery is.

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: I heard gunfire, and I heard some voices that were not understandable for me from the direction of the mosque. Then, at about 5.00, there was an explosion in the direction of the mosque, then everything went quiet. Then at about 6.30 or 7.00, strong gunfire was heard from the direction of the cemetery and the direction of the school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So from the direction of the road of Donji Ahmic, Lower Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: Yes, from the main road, the direction of the cemetery and Donji Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you came out in front of your house with Mirko. What happened when you heard the gunfire?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: Well, I ran into the basement. I was frightened. He was somewhere around the house. We were afraid, we were surprised, because we had no idea what it was, where it came from, or what the shooting was. Then after that, Mirko and some others were there next to my shed, and I can say who they were. They were Dragan Samija, Mirko Sakic, Milutin Vidovic, Miro Samija. I can't remember everybody because I was afraid at the time. So they went from my house to a depression in order to stay there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that day when there was the gunfire, did you hear shooting afterwards, or only in the morning? Did it go on for a while?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: Well, it went on until the afternoon hours. Then sometime towards the evening, it quieted down almost completely. While it was going on, I could see -- just below my house there's a side road, I could see people passing, fleeing their homes, the Muslims who were living in Donja Zume. They were going towards Gornji Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did those people pass?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: Well, I can't tell you the time. They were passing throughout the day in ones or twos, you could see them. From my house, my neighbour Refik Ahmic, he was making apple jam all day -- we call it pekmiz (phoen) in Bosnia -- so he didn't leave his house all day. That's this house right here (indicating).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the rest of your Muslim neighbours? You said that there were some other neighbours there, Sulejman Ahmic?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: He doesn't live there. He lives in Vitez, and he had a house there where he would come occasionally. He didn't live there all the time. He had an apartment in Vitez. That was his house. When a person retires -- well, that's what he used to say because we grew up together, went to school together, and we know each other well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The other neighbours, the Bilics, the Strmonjas, do you know whether they fled?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: Yes, they went to the shelter, but to the house of Vidovic, because it was closer to them, only some 300 metres. My shelter is small, some 16 or 18 square metres, and not everybody could fit in.

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: In the first conflicts, did the Bilics flee from Ahmici, that is, from Pirici?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You saw them there?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: Yes, we saw them in front of their house. They were at home. That evening I happened to pass by, and I had a chat with Ramo, because his family was there and everybody was there. Their brother, who works in Austria, had a house, and his son-in-law, Miralem Strmonja, was living there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 20th of October, did you see Mirjan and Zoran Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: Mirjan and Zoran Kupreskic were in the depression too, and their family, their father and mother, went to Jozo Vrebac's shelter with the children. After that, they went to their sister's, Zorica's, in Santici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: They told me that. The following day, there was no shooting anymore, and they told me that their children and their wives and their father and mother were there, their sister, and they didn't come back until the Muslims started coming back to their houses because they were afraid. They had five small children. The father and the mother were in poor health. They wanted to protect them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you on good terms with their father, Anto Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: I grew up together with their father, and we knew each other since we were children. We knew each other all our lives until he died. I know that it's a family which was poor. They were not prosperous. They lived in difficult circumstances. They had children whom they educated, and they made sacrifices to educate their children. They were a patriarchal family. They never deviated from their traditions. They lived in family harmony, such as everybody might wish for, and that's how they lived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did their father die, Anto Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: In '93, in August or September. He was a good friend of mine, but I can't remember the exact month when he died. It was either in August or September. I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did he die of?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: Well, he was so worried about his children. He was so upset by the war and all these events, and his health was very poor anyway, so perhaps this speeded up his death.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What speeded up his death? I didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: Well, the whole situation such as it was. He wanted the war to end, and that's why he was so worried.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Let us now return to the 20th of October, the first conflict. Did any of your neighbours, who lived around your house -- who were in your house and whom you saw that day, use weapons in any way against the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: I can affirm with certainty that they didn't, because had any of them used weapons -- can I show the house where this man was making jam and he stayed there the whole day?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: Well, you see, this is my house, my son's house, and this is Refik Ahmic's house and his brother's house. This whole plot of land belonged to them. Here you can see the fence around my house, and he was there making jam the whole day. He never left the place. So had there been any shooting, of course, he would have left. He wouldn't have known what had happened, so he would have left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. But there was gunfire elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: Yes, the gunfire came from the direction of the cemetery --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The cemetery is not there. Mr. Sakic, please concentrate. I see that you are nervous. Please take your time. You are showing Vlatko Kupreskic's house and saying it's the cemetery.

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: No. Just let me find it. This is the cemetery. Here it is (indicating). So from the direction of the cemetery and the school and the mosque, we could hear gunfire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much. You may sit down. The Muslims who left, you saw yourself that some of the Muslims left the village and went in the direction of Upper Ahmici. Do you know when they came back?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: After two or three days. They returned two or three days later. Individuals would come to tend to their remaining livestock, to fetch food, but within three days, they all returned to their houses. When they returned, the family of Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic and their father and mother also returned to their house because they live on the right-hand side where all the people are Muslims. Vlatko Kupreskic also lives there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the meetings which were held in the village after the first conflict?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: After the first conflict, Hazim Ahmic, Hadzija, invited me personally. I went twice to the school, so that the ordinary people might help to ease the tension.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please continue carefully? How many meetings were there?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: There were three meetings. I attended two of them, and I wasn't present at one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were the meetings held?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: They were held in the school across from Hazim's house and across the street from the mosque.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You said that you were invited by Hazim Ahmic personally.

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: Once, yes, and the second time, I happened to see people going there from Santici, so I joined the group, but no one invited me personally to go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
