utterances.text: Could you tell the Court how many people were present at these meetings? Can you establish the number of people?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: Well, there were about 150 of us. There were about 65 to 70 Croats and the rest were Muslims. There may have been more people, but that's what I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it like this at the second meeting -- wait until I finish my question, please. At the second meeting, was there such a large number of people?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: At the second meeting, there were even more people. At the meeting in the school where we were trying --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Can you tell us who chaired these meetings?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: The first meeting I attended was not attended by anyone from a political party, but the meeting started spontaneously. People said, "What's going on? How can we stop this? How can we continue living as we did before?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: The Muslims and the Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember if anyone chaired the meeting?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: As I said, no one chaired the first meeting, but the second meeting was attended by the representatives of the political authorities, Mr. Pero Skopljak, Mr. Kajmovic from the SDA party. I can't remember his first name. I know his surname was Kajmovic. There was Pero -- no, sorry, Ivica Santic. I asked them why, at the democratic elections when the government was elected, why things weren't going as they should. Pero Skopljak said to me, "The Bosniak Muslim side will not agree to the propositions of the elections," and Mr. Kajmovic said something that I could not understand. I didn't know what he was talking about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I didn't understand what you said just now. What did you ask him?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: What did I say?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you ask?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: I said, "Why isn't power distributed democratically according to the election results?" He said to me, Mr. Skopljak, that the Muslim side would not agree to this, and Mr. Kajmovic gave me such a vague reply that I can't remember what he said because he didn't give me a proper answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any other people take part in the discussion? What standpoints were put forward? What conclusions were reached?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: Well, everything boiled down to the fact that the conflict should not escalate, and there were people who were Bosniak Muslims who were a little more aggressive and who tried to expel the Muslims from the meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does that mean? What are you trying to say?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: What I want to say is that they wanted to break up the meeting. They wanted to dissolve the meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: Individual Muslims, Suad Ahmic and Sulejman Ahmic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was their political affiliation, the two that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: Well, they spoke untruths which were not accepted by the local Muslims. They said that this was not true, and they wanted to expel them from the meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wait a little. Can you say whether the two people you are referring to expressed opinions which were not shared by most of the other Muslims? Is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: No, they didn't say that. What they wanted -- for example, Suad Ahmic, he even said that the Muslims were not being sold cigarettes by the Croats, and the others said, "No, that's not true. We bought cigarettes from Muslims, and they sold them to us," and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So these two were extremists?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: Yes, they were extremists, more extreme than the normal people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. How did this meeting end?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: It ended by us saying that we should reduce the tension, ease the tension among the people, but as to anything else, I did not hear that anything else was agreed on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this meeting, was there any talk about returning weapons?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I don't know who had weapons or not, but there was no discussion of handing in weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know when the last meeting took place approximately? Can you place the other two in time?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: No, I can't tell you when any of the meetings took place, but I think they all took place within a period of 10 to 12 days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long was this after the conflict; can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: The conflict was on the 20th of October, and this was after about -- I think it was in January of the following year that these meetings took place, in January 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you sure of this?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: No, I'm not sure because I don't remember the dates. I can't be certain it was then. I attended two of the meetings, but I can't tell you the dates.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would there be any point in reducing the tensions which happened in October in January? Would that make sense?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: No. No, it wouldn't make sense. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is it possible that these meetings were held earlier?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: Yes, but, as I say, I can't say when.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You said that Pero Skopljak and Ivica Santic were at the meetings. Do you know if Kajmovic, whom you mentioned, was at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: The first time I saw the man was then, and they said that he was representing the SDA political party. I don't know what his position was in the party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Pero Skopljak?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: I don't know what Pero Skopljak's post was. I heard that he was a member of the HDZ because the people said, "Oh, well, now the representatives of the parties are here," but I don't know what his position was. Even today, I don't know who is who in the government.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ivica Santic, do you know what he was at that time?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: I don't know. I know that later he was the mayor, but what he was then, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he the president of the municipality then too?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Can you tell us whether you ever joined the village guards?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: I took part in the guards, and that was a spontaneous village patrol. I participated twice with the late Anto Kupreskic, Zoran and Mirjan's father. I had a hunting rifle. He didn't have anything. So on one occasion, he said to me, "Let's stretch our legs. Let's take a walk and patrol the village." It wasn't obligatory, and these patrols took place to prevent looting or burning or something like that, but no one had to go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The hunting rifle you said you have, whose gun is that? Whose rifle is that?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: It's my father's rifle. My father was a hunter. He had a proper license. Later, it was registered in the name of my son, Mirko, who is a hunter, and I'm keeping it as a souvenir, a memento of my father, in the house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that's the rifle that's registered to your son?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: Yes, to Mirko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your part of the village, which television programme could you follow?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: I could only receive, and my close neighbours, we could receive television from Sarajevo, the television of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We couldn't receive any other television programmes. Because up until recently, I had a black and white television, so I really couldn't receive any other programmes, except for those two channels on Bosnia-Herzegovina Television.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But did other people say that they were watching Television Vitez?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: Yes. People would say that, and I tried to find it, but I could never tune in. Some people said that they could, but I didn't, so I can't really tell you anything about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the news from Television Vitez, you couldn't receive that?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: No. No, I could never tune into that, so I couldn't watch that news.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anybody from your neighbourhood say that they could watch Television Vitez, from those houses around yours?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: Those people who I had woken up and who were close to my house never told me that they could watch that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 15th of April, 1993, that was the day before the war broke out in the Lasva Valley, so that was the day before the conflict, did you get any kind of information that something was about to happen, that something was being prepared, that some measures needed to be taken, some cautionary measures, since you were in the civilian defence?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: Yes. I received information at 4.00 in the morning. At 4.00 in the morning on the 16th, Dragan Vidovic came to me and said, "There is an announcement that we will be attacked by the Muslims," that we should go to the certain shelters which I mentioned before, the population should go there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the day before.

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: No. The day before, I didn't know anything. The whole day, I was working as usual, just like everyone else, and I didn't know anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 16th, in the morning, you said that Dragan Vidovic came, and what did he say to you?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: He said that he had heard information that there is the possibility of us being attacked by the Muslims and that we should go to shelters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you that you needed to inform anybody or not?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: Well, he told me to inform those people that I would usually inform, for them to go to the basement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you informed your neighbours?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: Yes, I informed my son Mirko, Slavko's family, the family of my son Slavko, Nikola Omazic, Nikola Samija, Drago Grgic, Miro Samija, Mirjan Samija, Anto Pudza, and Slavko Pudza. I went to the houses of Zijad and Rano Bilic and their son-in-law, Miralem. I woke them up, and they crossed over to the shelter in Niko Vidovic's house with their families.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you sure that you woke them up?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who are those people? Are they Croats or Muslims?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: They're Muslims. Ramo Bilic, Zijad Bilic, with their families, and their son-in-law, Miralem Strmonja, they're all Muslims by religion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you wake them up?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: Well, when I left from my house, I woke everybody up that I mentioned, and then I also went to them to wake them up. That was right after Dragan told me. At 4.00, of course, I woke up my own family, and then I went to wake up everybody else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you wake up or inform by telephone anybody else, or what did you do?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: I didn't have a telephone at the time. My son upstairs had a telephone, but his entrance was on the other side of the house. So I didn't have a telephone at the time, so I couldn't wake up anybody by telephone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you go then, after you woke all of your neighbours up?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: When I woke my neighbours, the ones that I mentioned, then I was standing there, surprised, in front of my house. I didn't know what was going to happen, where, what kind of an attack. Then from the direction of Zume --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time was this, approximately?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: This was at about 4.30, when I woke everybody up and came back home, at about 4.30.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your son come down?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: Yes, my son Mirko came down first. Then after a while my daughter-in-law with the children came, then Slavko's family also came to the basement, and those that I mentioned came to the basement, except for the Bilics, who went to the other basement, which was closer to them and where there was more room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. All of these families came to the basement, you said; is that right? The men and the women, they came to your house? Where did the men go, and where did the women go?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: The men and the women came to my house. The men went above the house, next to the garage, my garage. And from there they went towards the depression, the one near my house, and the women and the children and the elderly went to the shelter. Should I say who was there in the depression?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, you don't need to say who was in which depression. Just tell me, how many people did come to your basement, and how big is that basement?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: Well, in normal conditions, you can't have too many people there, but there were more than it could fit. The basement is small. It's about 16 or 18 square metres. So only a few people could fit in there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was the first gunfire heard? Can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: The first gunfire could be heard at about 5.30, from the direction of Middle Ahmici: The school, the main road, and -- the school and the mosque. That's the main road. Then also from the direction of the Kupreskic houses, that's where the firing came from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "Middle Ahmici," what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: I mean that the way the road goes and the way the village is situated, you have the beginning of the village, the centre of the village, and then the end. That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So which would be the central part? Could you please show us that? So that's the main road?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: Yes. Just one moment. Here (indicating). These are the Kupreskic houses, Vlatko's house, near Vlatko's warehouse. That's where the central part of Ahmici is. Then the rest goes above the Kupreskic houses, and then the other part goes from behind -- after the road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the gunfire could be heard from that entire area?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: Yes, from the entire area, but it was the strongest in these three places.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you determine when you saw Mirjan and Zoran Kupreskic for the first time that morning?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult to say precisely, but I can say that I saw Mirjan's father and mother. They were going -- Mirjan was pushing his mother-in-law in a wheelbarrow in front of the Pudza houses, and his wife was leading the children. Then Zoran came. Zoran was going before him. Zoran was taking his family, his three children and his wife.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did they go? Mr. Sakic, if you can just concentrate, you are indicating the direction towards Vlatko's house. Could you please pay attention to where you are pointing. Could you point in which direction they were going, from where to where?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: This is where I saw them (indicating).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Is that your house?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So now will you please indicate the road that they were going along?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: They were going along this road (indicating).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were going towards where?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: They were going towards the house of Jozo Vrebac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So could you please show us with the pointer, which direction were they going?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: They were going from the house towards the shelter of Jozo Vrebac. These are the Kupreskic houses (indicating).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, those can't be Kupreskic houses. You indicated nicely before. Do you see the white section that you can see on the photograph?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: Yes, this part. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is the warehouse of Vlatko?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: Yes, that's Vlatko's warehouse. They came from the warehouse through this path. There is a pedestrian path there. They were going in the direction of the shelter of Jozo Vrebac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So where did they pass?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: They go this way (indicating). They're going here, this way (indicating). So that's where the house is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they're going from the Kupreskic houses, the road past your house in the direction of the shelter, okay. You may sit down. Thank you. So you saw them in the morning. Did you see them before the gunfire broke out or after that? Was there firing when they were passing or not?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: No, there was no firing when they were passing. When they passed, there was no gunfire at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you at that time?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: I was in front of the house, in front of my yard. My yard is large, so I was next to the road itself. I wasn't in the middle of the road, but I was right next to the road. That's where I was standing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who was with you there? Who was standing close to you at that time?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: At that time, my son Mirko was standing with me. I don't know if there was anybody else, but I know about him for sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any other people next to your house? Can you remember?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: Well, Dragan Samija was there, Miro Vidovic, near the garage. Zdravko Vrebac -- I can't remember everybody now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So some people were there. You remember your son?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: Yes, I remember him and the people that I mentioned. There were others, but I've forgotten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you sure about Zdravko Vrebac?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: I don't know. I think that he was there, but I -- I know exactly my Mirko was there, but for the others, I'm not sure, at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did you see, in that section of the village, any soldiers?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: In the area around my house, yes. Some soldiers passed from my house towards the warehouse, that way, maybe 30 or 35 soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did you see the direction that those soldiers came from?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: No, I didn't see. They came from the direction of Zume. As much as I can see the road in front of my house, it's in the direction of Zume.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did those soldiers look?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: They were painted -- their faces were painted. They were well armed. They each had two weapons. I didn't see what kind it was. They passed by us next to my garage and went towards Vlatko's warehouse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you frightened by that army?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: Yes, I was frightened. I was frightened the whole time anyway. I don't know how I survived from that fear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why were you afraid? Who did you think that army was?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: Well, I could see their markings. I didn't think about anything else, just about my fear. At that moment, I couldn't think of anything else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did those soldiers go?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: They went in the direction of the warehouse of Vlatko Kupreskic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were they going? In a file, in a column?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: Yes, they were going in a group, as if they were walking down the street, five or six of them, or ten in a group, or two or three. So that was the formation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they loud or quiet?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: They weren't talking at all. They just passed by us. No one said anything to me, nor did I recognise any one of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did the gunfire start in relation to when they departed? After they left, how soon after that did the gunfire begin?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: Well, the gunfire started at about 5.30. From the direction of the Kupreskic houses, you could hear it, you could hear it from the school, and also from the main road, the Travnik-Sarajevo road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see Zoran and Mirjan coming again from the direction of Zume in which they had left? Did you see them coming back?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: When they took their families there, Mirjan remained at my house and Zoran took the Didaks, refugees, Manda, Marica, and their children, and took them in the direction of Zume.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, how long did you stand in front of your house?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: Well, I didn't stay there all the time. I would go to the shelter occasionally, but I spent more time outside as long as there was no gunfire. And I could see that well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So as long as there was no shooting, you were outside. So you went to the shelter when?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: When the gunfire became intense, then I went to the shelter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the shelter, did you stay there the whole time, or did you leave?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: I left from time to time, because the father and mother of Dragan Vidovic and their family were there, and his mother asked me to go and see where their children were, what they were doing and how they were. They were about 40 metres or 50 metres, at the most, from my house. From time to time they would come to see their family and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were they in relation to your house, and who do you mean by "they"?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: In the depression, there were Mirko Sakic, my son; Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic; Miro Pudza; Dragan Samija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see them when you went out of your house?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: No, I had to go around my house and come to the garage above my house, and I would see them from there because it's a depression and you can look into it from that spot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go to the garage to see how they were doing and where they were?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: Yes, I went there several times during the day, and I saw them in the valley, in the depression. Zoran Kupreskic and my son Mirko would come to the house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you saw them, when you were standing in front of the garage and looking down into the depression, what were they doing in the depression?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: They were just sitting there, or standing, in various positions. Because you couldn't see very well from the depression, but it's protected, so that you could not be hit by a weapon unless a bomb was dropped from the air straight above it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see them shooting at anyone?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: No, I didn't see them shooting at anyone, nor could they have shot at anyone from there. They could only shoot up into the air. You couldn't shoot from there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: Because it's like being in a jug, so it's impossible to shoot at anyone from there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So on that day, you saw them several times? That's what you said?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: Yes, I saw them several times. They would come up to the house. Mirko and Zoran came several times. The others came in front of the house, too, but I know those two very well, and on the telephone as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know anything about Mirjan Santic?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: They brought Mirjan Santic to my garage, dead, on a ladder. He was brought there by Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic, Nikola Omaric, and Dragan Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was Mirjan Santic killed?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: They told me that he was killed near the Kupreskic houses. I don't know exactly where, but that's what they told me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long was Mirjan Santic in the garage?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: Maybe about ten minutes, because they had a close relative, Milan Samija and Miro, in a house nearby, so they took him to the house of their son-in-law, Stipo Brnada, and I don't know what happened then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that is the house they moved him to, the house of Stipo Brnada?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: That man is in Germany. He was taken away by Milan Samija and Miro Samija, with Milan's wife. The four of them took him away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On what day was Mirjan Santic killed?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: The first day, the 16th, when the conflict broke out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you certain of this?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC.
utterances.text: I'm certain. I know it was the first day. I'm sure of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think we can stop here, and I will finish very quickly tomorrow. Thank you.
